prompt: What question does a blameless postmortem replace "who made the mistake?" with?

choices.text: Who should have noticed?
choices.why: Still a question about a person to blame.

choices.text: How much did it cost?
choices.why: Impact is recorded, and it is not the central question.

choices.text: How did it make sense to them?
choices.why: Right. People did what made sense with what they knew.

choices.text: Which team owns the system?
choices.why: Ownership matters for actions, not as the question.

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: the circumstances that made the error likely
the path to failure looking obvious afterwards

prompt: Why does a blameless postmortem produce better facts?

choices.text: People who expect to be understood omit less
choices.why: Right. "I thought it was the usual noise" is the sentence that matters.

choices.text: Because nobody is allowed to speak about people
choices.why: People are discussed; blame is what is set aside.

choices.text: Because the logs are more complete
choices.why: The logs are the same; what people say changes.

choices.text: Because it is written by an outside auditor
choices.why: It is written by the team.

prompt: Does blameless mean that nobody is ever responsible for anything?

choices.text: Yes; that is the point of the word
choices.why: Responsibility is placed where it does good, on the system and its owners.

choices.text: Yes, except for managers
choices.why: Nothing in it exempts or targets managers.

choices.text: No; the most junior person is held responsible
choices.why: That is blame, aimed downwards.

choices.text: No; recklessness still counts
choices.why: Right. The default for everything else is the second story.

prompt: What is the weakness of asking "why" five times about a whole incident?

choices.text: Five is too few questions
choices.why: The count is not the problem.

choices.text: It follows only one chain
choices.why: Right. Use it on each contributing factor instead.

choices.text: It always ends at a person
choices.why: It can end anywhere; its limit is following one chain.

choices.text: It cannot be done in a meeting
choices.why: It can; it is just incomplete.

prompt: Which of these were contributing factors in the 30 September incident? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: The retry had no idempotency key
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing alerted on duplicate charges
choices.why: Right. Seventeen minutes until a customer called.

choices.text: The release reached every shop at once
choices.why: Right. A partial release would have limited it.

choices.text: The team had no incident commander
choices.why: Bia took command at 17:49.

prompt: A postmortem finds that Duda approved the faulty change. What does the lesson say comes next?

choices.text: Duda reviews more carefully from now on
choices.why: The next reviewer will not be Duda; the fix must be in the system.

choices.text: The analysis ends: the cause is found
choices.why: Human error is where analysis starts.

choices.text: Ask what made approving it seem right
choices.why: Right. Here: the checklist did not ask about retries.

choices.text: Reviews are removed, since they failed
choices.why: Reviews catch many problems; this one needed a better prompt.

prompt: Instead of one root cause, a good postmortem lists every contributing ___.
Put the first sections of the postmortem document in the order of the lesson's template.
Why keep the timeline separate from the analysis?

choices.text: Hindsight would creep into the timeline
choices.why: Right. "The faulty release was deployed" was not known at 17:20.

choices.text: Because they are written by different teams
choices.why: The same people write both.

choices.text: Because timelines are confidential
choices.why: They are published with the rest.

choices.text: Because the analysis is optional
choices.why: It is the heart of the document.

prompt: Where do names belong in a postmortem document?

choices.text: Nowhere, to keep it blameless
choices.why: Names on actions are needed; somebody has to own them.

choices.text: On the contributing factors
choices.why: That turns factors into accusations.

choices.text: Only in the summary
choices.why: The summary is for strangers; it needs no names.

choices.text: On actions only
choices.why: Right. "Rafa will add an idempotency key by 9 October."

prompt: Why honour a request for a postmortem even when the incident looked small?

choices.text: Because every incident must have one
choices.why: The rule is SEV1, SEV2 and requests, not every incident.

choices.text: The person asking saw something real
choices.why: Right. Near misses that frightened people are where much of the learning is.

choices.text: Because postmortems improve the DORA metrics
choices.why: Not directly, and not the reason.

choices.text: Because refusing would look bad
choices.why: Appearance is not the argument.

prompt: actions.py reports 8 action items due and 4 of those done. What is the completion rate, in percent?
Which open action item would most likely have caught the 30 September incident within minutes?

choices.text: Write a runbook for rolling back a release
choices.why: The rollback was already quick; this is mitigation, not detection.

choices.text: Fix the flaky refund test
choices.why: That one was done, and unrelated.

choices.text: The alert on charges per minute
choices.why: Right. Due 14 September, still open on 30 September.

choices.text: Integration test for the statement export
choices.why: Done in August, and about another feature.

prompt: The rollback runbook from D004 was due on 3 July. How many days overdue was it on 2 October?
Match each action item to its kind.

pairs.left: idempotency key on every card retry
add retries to the review checklist

prompt: Why do action items so often lose to planned work?

choices.text: No room was left for them
choices.why: Right. Lesson 12's slack is where they belong.

choices.text: Because they are less important
choices.why: Three of the Billing team's would have prevented an incident.

choices.text: Because they are never written down
choices.why: They are written; they are not done.

choices.text: Because managers forbid them
choices.why: Nobody forbids them; nobody makes room.

prompt: "Release to 5% of shops before the rest" sat undone for 48 days. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Drop it, since it is too big
choices.why: It would have limited a real incident; it is worth doing.

choices.text: Give it a later due date
choices.why: Moving the date does not make it startable.

choices.text: Assign it to the whole team
choices.why: One owner, not the team.

choices.text: Split off a one-day first step
choices.why: Right. Such as deciding how to route 5% of shops.

prompt: Why ask "what did the review look at?" rather than "why did you approve that?"

choices.text: Because "why" questions are rude in every culture
choices.why: Culture is not the argument; how the question is heard is.

choices.text: "Why" questions are heard as accusations
choices.why: Right. Questions about the situation get full answers.

choices.text: Because the facilitator already knows why
choices.why: Nobody knows until they ask.

choices.text: Because reviews are confidential
choices.why: They are discussed openly.

prompt: Who should ideally facilitate the postmortem meeting?

choices.text: The incident commander, who knows it best
choices.why: Her decisions are under examination.

choices.text: The person who wrote the faulty change
choices.why: They are a participant, not a chair.

choices.text: The most senior manager available
choices.why: Seniority invites a trial.

choices.text: Somebody who was not the commander
choices.why: Right. It is hard to examine your own decisions while chairing.

prompt: Three open action items would each have made the 30 September incident smaller. What single number would have shown the risk before it happened?

choices.text: The change failure rate
choices.why: It was low in September; it said nothing about this.

choices.text: The number of incidents per month
choices.why: It counts what happened, not what was left undone.

choices.text: The action item completion rate
choices.why: Right. Half done, with the overdue ones listed.

choices.text: The deployment frequency
choices.why: It rose in September and hid nothing about this.

prompt: After the postmortem, what are the shops that were double-charged owed?

choices.text: An explanation and what will change
choices.why: Right. In their terms, as well as the refund.

choices.text: Nothing beyond the refund
choices.why: They were owed an explanation too.

choices.text: The full postmortem with its timeline
choices.why: Too internal; they need what matters to them.

choices.text: The name of whoever was responsible
choices.why: Blameless outward as well as inward.
